name: EV Charging (Level 2, Home)
blurb: Home EV charging typically adds 250–400 kWh a month for average driving — often the single largest new line on the bill, yet still far cheaper per mile than gasoline. Your state's electricity rate is the entire story: the same commute costs nearly four times more to charge in Hawaii than North Dakota.
tips: Enroll in your utility's EV or time-of-use plan — overnight rates can halve charging cost.
Schedule charging in the car or charger app rather than plugging in at 6 pm peak.
Preconditioning while plugged in shifts cabin heating/cooling energy off the battery and onto cheaper wall power.

name: Electric Lawn Mower
blurb: Charging a battery mower for a typical suburban lawn uses 1–2 kWh per mow — a few dimes even in expensive states. Across a season, electric mowing costs a small fraction of gas, before counting oil and maintenance.

name: Electric Leaf Blower
blurb: Corded blowers draw around 900 watts and battery models use half a kilowatt-hour or less per session. A fall's worth of leaf cleanup costs less than a cup of coffee.

name: Electric Snow Blower
blurb: Electric snow blowers draw 1,500–2,500 watts working hard, using a couple of kilowatt-hours per driveway clearing. Even a snowy month's clearings cost a dollar or two — the driveway workout is free.

name: Air Compressor
blurb: Garage compressors draw 1,000–2,200 watts while the motor runs, but duty cycles are short — the tank does the work between refills. Occasional tire and nailer use costs pennies; constant leaks that force refill cycles are the hidden cost.

name: Welder (Home Shop)
blurb: A 240 V hobby welder can draw several kilowatts mid-arc, but actual arc-on time in a weekend project is minutes, not hours. Even regular hobby welding rarely adds more than a few dollars a month.

name: Table Saw
blurb: A contractor table saw pulls about 1,800 watts under load, but cutting time in a typical project is brief. A serious weekend in the wood shop — saw, dust collector, sander — usually totals a single kilowatt-hour or two.

name: Shop Vac
blurb: Shop vacuums draw 1,000–1,400 watts of loud suction, in short bursts. Cleanup after projects amounts to cents per month — buy for filtration and capacity, not efficiency.

name: Garage Door Opener
blurb: Opening the door uses trivial energy; the surprise is standby. Older openers idle at 5–10 watts around the clock waiting for the remote — often 50 times more energy per year than the actual lifting.

name: Electric Patio Heater
blurb: Infrared patio heaters draw 900–3,000 watts and heat people directly, so effectiveness outdoors depends on distance and wind. An evening under one costs about what an indoor space heater would — but the sky gets most of the warmth.

name: Bug Zapper
blurb: Bug zappers run 20–100 watts through summer evenings. A season of nightly operation costs a few dollars — though studies find they mostly kill harmless insects while mosquitoes ignore them.

name: Electric Pressure Washer
blurb: Electric pressure washers draw 1,300–1,800 watts while spraying. Washing the car or deck uses well under a kilowatt-hour — the water bill notices before the electric bill does.

name: Electric Smoker
blurb: Electric smokers hold low temperatures with an 500–1,500 watt element cycling over many hours, so a long brisket smoke uses several kilowatt-hours. Still cheaper than a bag of lump charcoal in most states.

name: E-Bike Charging
blurb: Charging a typical 500 Wh e-bike battery from empty costs a few cents in every state — pennies per 20–40 miles of range. Per mile, an e-bike is roughly ten times cheaper than an EV and fifty times cheaper than a gas car.

name: Electric Scooter Charging
blurb: E-scooter batteries hold 250–500 Wh, so a full charge costs a nickel or less nearly everywhere. Commuting by scooter all month adds less to a bill than one load of laundry.
